note: Revised from Emerson's (1928) description of the species, originally in English; the alate and the soldier have morphological descriptions and the queen is given only measurements; the measurement of head length with mandibles in the soldier is incomplete in the scanned text and was not recorded; the worker and nymph are not described in the original. Figure numbers, localities and records of inquiline beetle larvae have been omitted.

sections.label: Soldier
sections.text: Head reddish yellow, oval to rectangular, sides rounded; antennae 13-segmented, the third segment smallest, almost as long as the second, the fourth wider and longer than the third; mandibles reddish brown, stout, strongly and irregularly serrate; anterior margin of the pronotum slightly excavated or not at all, the notch sometimes filled by a small transparent lamina. Measurements: head width 1.10–1.15, antenna length 1.67, pronotum length 0.33, width 0.72–0.75, hind tibia 0.90–1.00, left mandible 1.20.

sections.label: Alate
sections.text: Head pale yellowish brown, slightly quadrate, sides straight and parallel; fontanelle small, concolorous with the head; the third antennal segment small, the fourth slightly shorter than the second; compound eyes medium-sized, not protruding, rather close to the lower margin of the head; ocelli small, separated from the compound eye by less than their own width; postclypeus paler than the head, with a median suture. Pronotum slightly paler than the head, posterior margin slightly incised, its width about equal to the head width including the eyes; posterior margins of mesonotum and metanotum broadly incised. Measurements: head length 1.23, head width 1.10, eye diameter 0.32, pronotum length 0.60, width 0.99, hind tibia 1.11.

sections.label: Other
sections.text: Queen body length 20.00, abdominal width 3.00. Nests are built as large carton nests on branches of Ficus congoensis; there are also dark brown clay nests in the forks of mango trees, about 8 feet above the ground, with numerous covered galleries on the trunk connected to the nest. Nest shape and structure are very irregular and vary with the supporting branches, and the nests resemble those of black ants; they consist of very irregular cells, generally one-third to one-half of an inch wide, with very thin walls, one-sixteenth of an inch or less; the nest is hard but relatively light, greyish brown outside and dark brown inside; the lower surface bears stalactite-like projections, some of them nearly hollow to the base.
